discovery.title: Could a tiny sample from Phobos explain how Mars got its moons?
discovery.summary: Japan’s MMX spacecraft is scheduled to launch on October 20 JST, aiming to study Mars’s moons and return a Phobos sample to Earth. The mission could help test whether the moons formed from a Mars-impact event or were captured asteroids.
discovery.why_it_matters: A sample could reshape ideas about how planetary systems form and inform future exploration of Mars and its moons.

discovery.title: Parents say babies matter—but do they think help is worth the cost?
discovery.summary: A University of Michigan national poll reports that 81% of parents say having a baby is more expensive than it should be, while 59% say supporting families with young children is a good use of taxpayer dollars.
discovery.why_it_matters: The contrast highlights a real-world tension between household financial pressure and public support for early-childhood programs.

discovery.title: What could a million-gigabit cable change about the internet?
discovery.summary: A report published October 17 describes a planned 4,300-mile subsea cable designed to carry data at a reported capacity of one million gigabits per second. The project illustrates how internet infrastructure increasingly depends on cables laid across the ocean floor.
discovery.why_it_matters: More undersea capacity could affect cloud services, AI workloads, and the resilience of international data links, while leaving deployment and redundancy questions.

discovery.title: Are Mars’s moons captured asteroids—or debris from an ancient impact?
discovery.summary: Ahead of the MMX launch, mission explainers note that Phobos and Deimos may be captured asteroids or remnants of an impact involving Mars. MMX plans to study the moons and return material from Phobos for analysis.
discovery.why_it_matters: The moons’ origin could reveal how Mars evolved and clarify whether similar small bodies are captured or formed through collisions elsewhere in the Solar System.
